q: For which positive integer n is (n + 1)! = 20 × (n − 1)!?
x: (n + 1)! = (n + 1)n(n − 1)!, so n(n + 1) = 20 and n = 4 (the other root −5 is not allowed). Check: 5! = 120 and 20 × 3! = 120. Solving n + 1 = 20 gives 19.

q: How many three-digit numbers have all three digits different?
x: Hundreds digit: 9 choices (not 0); tens: 9 (any except the first, 0 now allowed); units: 8. Total 9 × 9 × 8 = 648. Check: 900 three-digit numbers minus 252 with a repeated digit (9 + 243) gives 648. Using 10 × 9 × 8 counts numbers starting with 0 and gives 720.

q: How many of the integers from 1 to 100 are divisible by neither 2 nor 5?
x: Divisible by 2: 50; by 5: 20; by both (by 10): 10. So 50 + 20 − 10 = 60 are divisible by 2 or 5, and 100 − 60 = 40 are divisible by neither. Check: in each block of 10 only the units digits 1, 3, 7, 9 qualify, 4 × 10 = 40. Forgetting to add back the 10 gives 30.

q: What is the value of 0! + 1! + 2! + 3!?
x: 0! = 1, 1! = 1, 2! = 2 and 3! = 6, so the sum is 1 + 1 + 2 + 6 = 10. Taking 0! = 0 gives 9.

q: With how many zeros does 25! end?
x: Each final zero needs a factor 10 = 2 × 5, and factors 5 are the scarcer. The multiples of 5 up to 25 give 25/5 = 5 fives, and 25 = 5² gives one more, so there are 6 zeros. Forgetting the extra 5 in 25 gives 5.

q: Bilal has 3 shirts, 4 trousers and 2 pairs of shoes. One of the shirts does not go with 2 of the trousers. How many complete outfits (shirt, trousers, shoes) can he wear?
x: Without the restriction there are 3 × 4 × 2 = 24 outfits. The banned ones are that shirt with either of the 2 trousers and any shoes: 1 × 2 × 2 = 4. So 24 − 4 = 20. Check directly: 2 × 4 × 2 + 1 × 2 × 2 = 16 + 4 = 20. Forgetting the shoes in the banned count gives 22.

q: How many positive divisors of 360 are even?
x: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5. An even divisor has 2ᵃ with a = 1, 2 or 3 (3 choices), 3ᵇ with b = 0, 1, 2 (3 choices) and 5ᶜ with c = 0, 1 (2 choices): 3 × 3 × 2 = 18. Check: 360 has 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 divisors, of which 3 × 2 = 6 are odd, and 24 − 6 = 18.

q: The letters of the word MULTAN are arranged so that every arrangement begins with M and ends with N. How many such arrangements are there?
x: M and N are fixed at the ends, so only the middle four letters U, L, T, A are arranged: 4! = 24. Fixing only one end gives 5! = 120, and no restriction gives 6! = 720.

q: If P(n, 3) = 210, what is the value of n?
Four-digit numbers are formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 with no digit repeated. How many of them are divisible by 5?
x: A number divisible by 5 must end in 5 here (there is no 0). The other three places are filled from the remaining 5 digits: P(5, 3) = 5 × 4 × 3 = 60. 360 is the count of all such four-digit numbers.

q: The letters of the word EQUAL are arranged in a row. In how many arrangements do the vowels occupy the 1st, 3rd and 5th places?
x: The vowels E, U, A fill the three odd places in 3! = 6 ways and the consonants Q, L fill the two even places in 2! = 2 ways: 6 × 2 = 12. Counting only the vowels gives 6.

q: In how many ways can 4 men and 4 women sit around a round table so that no two men sit next to each other?
x: Seat the women first round the table: (4 − 1)! = 6 ways. This leaves 4 gaps between them, one man in each: 4! = 24 ways. Total 6 × 24 = 144. Treating the table as a row for the women (4! instead of 3!) gives 576.

q: Three-letter codes are made from the 26 letters A to Z, and letters may repeat. How many codes contain at least one repeated letter?
x: All codes: 26³ = 17576. Codes with three different letters: P(26, 3) = 26 × 25 × 24 = 15600. So 17576 − 15600 = 1976 have a repeat. Check: exactly two alike 3 × 26 × 25 = 1950, all three alike 26, total 1976.

q: In how many ways can 3 boys and 3 girls stand in a row so that boys and girls alternate?
x: The pattern is either BGBGBG or GBGBGB (2 ways). In each, the boys can be arranged in 3! = 6 ways and the girls in 3! = 6 ways: 2 × 6 × 6 = 72. Forgetting that the row may start with a girl gives 36.

q: For certain n and r, P(n, r) = 120 and C(n, r) = 20. What is r?
x: P(n, r) = r! × C(n, r), so r! = 120/20 = 6 and r = 3. Check: n = 6 gives P(6, 3) = 120 and C(6, 3) = 20. Reading r! = 6 as r = 6 is the usual trap.

q: Eight points lie in a plane, no three on one straight line. How many straight lines can be drawn, each through two of the points?
x: Each line is fixed by an unordered pair of points: C(8, 2) = 8 × 7/2 = 28. Counting ordered pairs gives P(8, 2) = 56.

q: In how many ways can 12 students be split into one group of 8 and one group of 4?
x: Choosing the 4 for the small group fixes the other 8: C(12, 4) = (12 × 11 × 10 × 9)/24 = 495. This is the same as C(12, 8). Doubling it for the two groups gives 990, but the groups have different sizes, so nothing is counted twice.

q: Five horizontal lines cross four vertical lines. How many rectangles have their sides on these lines?
x: A rectangle needs 2 of the horizontal lines and 2 of the vertical lines: C(5, 2) × C(4, 2) = 10 × 6 = 60. Using the sides of the small squares only (4 × 3 = 12) misses the larger rectangles.

q: A committee of 4 is chosen from 5 married couples so that no husband and wife are both on it. In how many ways can this be done?
x: First choose which 4 of the 5 couples are represented: C(5, 4) = 5. Then pick husband or wife from each: 2⁴ = 16. Total 5 × 16 = 80. Check: of the C(10, 4) = 210 committees, 130 contain at least one couple.

q: For 1 ≤ r ≤ n, which expression equals C(n, r)/C(n, r − 1)?
x: C(n, r)/C(n, r − 1) = [n!/(r!(n − r)!)] × [(r − 1)!(n − r + 1)!/n!] = (n − r + 1)/r. Check with n = 5, r = 2: C(5, 2)/C(5, 1) = 10/5 = 2 and (5 − 2 + 1)/2 = 2. The flipped fraction is the most common slip.

q: A box holds 4 red and 6 blue pens. In how many ways can 3 pens be chosen with at most one red pen?
x: No red: C(6, 3) = 20. Exactly one red: 4 × C(6, 2) = 4 × 15 = 60. Total 80. Check: C(10, 3) = 120, minus two red (6 × 6 = 36) and three red (4) gives 80. 60 counts only the one-red case.

q: A letter is chosen at random from the letters of the word STATISTICS. What is the probability that it is T?
x: STATISTICS has 10 letters and 3 of them are T, so the probability is 3/10. Dividing by the 5 different letters or by the 7 non-T letters gives the wrong options.

q: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the two numbers differ by exactly 2?
x: The pairs are (1, 3), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 6) and the same four reversed: 8 of the 36 outcomes, so 8/36 = 2/9. Forgetting the reversed pairs gives 4/36 = 1/9.

q: For events E and F, P(E) = 0.5, P(F) = 0.4 and P(E ∩ F) = 0.2. Which statement is true?
o: E and F are mutually exclusive
The probability that neither happens is 0.2
x: P(E)P(F) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2 = P(E ∩ F), so E and F are independent. E and F are not mutually exclusive since P(E ∩ F) ≠ 0. P(E ∪ F) = 0.5 + 0.4 − 0.2 = 0.7, so neither happens with probability 0.3.

q: A bag has 3 white and 5 black balls. Two balls are drawn together at random. What is the probability that they are of different colours?
x: Favourable: 3 × 5 = 15 pairs; total: C(8, 2) = 28. So 15/28. Check: 1 − P(both white) − P(both black) = 1 − 3/28 − 10/28 = 15/28. Using ordered draws for the total (56) but unordered for the favourable gives 15/56.

q: A three-digit number is formed at random from three different digits chosen from 1, 2, 3, 4. What is the probability that it is divisible by 4?
x: There are P(4, 3) = 24 numbers. Divisible by 4 means the last two digits form a multiple of 4: 12, 24 or 32. Each leaves 2 digits for the hundreds place, giving 6 numbers, so 6/24 = 1/4. Missing 32 gives 4/24 = 1/6.

q: A leap year is chosen at random. What is the probability that it has 53 Fridays?
x: 366 days = 52 weeks + 2 days, so there are 52 Fridays plus the 2 extra consecutive days. Of the 7 equally likely pairs (Sun-Mon, …, Sat-Sun), Thu-Fri and Fri-Sat contain a Friday: 2/7. A normal year with 1 extra day would give 1/7.

q: Ahmed and Bilal take turns rolling a fair die, Ahmed first. The first to roll a six wins. What is the probability that Ahmed wins?
x: Ahmed wins on his 1st, 2nd, 3rd … turn with probabilities 1/6, (5/6)²(1/6), (5/6)⁴(1/6), …, a G.P. with ratio 25/36. Sum = (1/6)/(1 − 25/36) = (1/6)(36/11) = 6/11. Check: Bilal then wins with 5/11, and 6/11 + 5/11 = 1.
